topics.title: 2026 Social Security Tax Cap: $184,500 - What High Earners Should Know
topics.script: If you're a higher earner, this 2026 number matters for your paycheck. The Social Security Administration just raised the taxable maximum, also called the wage base, to 184,500 dollars for 2026. That means Social Security tax, the 6.2 percent you see withheld from your paycheck, only applies up to that amount of income. Once your year to date wages cross 184,500 dollars, that specific withholding stops for the rest of the year. If you switch jobs mid year, double check your total withholding across employers, because each employer restarts the calculation separately, and you could end up overpaying. You'd then claim that excess back as a credit on your tax return.

topics.title: 2026 Capital Gains Tax Brackets: 0%, 15%, 20% - New IRS Thresholds
topics.script: Selling stock or property this year? The IRS just updated the income thresholds for long term capital gains taxes in 2026. If you're single and your taxable income is under 49,450 dollars, you pay zero percent tax on long term gains. Between 49,450 and 545,500, you pay 15 percent. Above that, it's 20 percent. If you're married filing jointly, the zero percent bracket goes up to 98,900 dollars, 15 percent applies up to 613,700, and 20 percent kicks in above that. This only applies to investments held more than a year. Short term gains are taxed as regular income instead. Knowing these numbers can help you time a sale, especially if you're near a bracket line. Talk to a tax professional before making a big move.

topics.title: 2026 Estate Tax Exemption Jumps to $15 Million - IRS Confirms
topics.script: Here's a number that matters if you're doing estate planning. For 2026, the IRS raised the federal estate tax exemption to 15 million dollars per person. That means an individual can pass on up to 15 million dollars at death without owing any federal estate tax, and a married couple can combine their exemptions to shield 30 million dollars. This higher exemption is now permanent under the new tax law, instead of scheduled to shrink like it was before. Only estates above these amounts owe federal estate tax, so this mainly affects high net worth families. Most states also have their own separate estate or inheritance tax rules with much lower thresholds. If your estate is anywhere near these numbers, work with an estate planning attorney now.

topics.script: Here's a tax rule that mostly targets higher earners with big deductions or incentive stock options. The exemption starts phasing out once income crosses 500,000 dollars for single filers, or 1 million dollars for married couples. This mostly affects people with large state tax deductions, exercised stock options, or big itemized deductions. If any of that applies to you, run the AMT calculation before you file.

If you installed and paid for qualifying upgrades by the end of 2025, you can still claim it on that year's tax return. Some states and utility companies still offer their own rebates, so check those before you assume there's no help available. Always confirm current incentives before starting a project.

topics.title: 2026 Medicare Part B Premium: $202.90 - IRMAA Brackets If You Earn More
topics.script: Retiring soon or already on Medicare? Here's your 2026 number from CMS. The standard Medicare Part B premium is now 202.90 dollars a month, up from 185 dollars, and the annual deductible rose to 283 dollars. But if your income is higher, you'll pay more through something called IRMAA, the income related monthly adjustment amount. For example, if you're single and your income was above 109,000 dollars two years ago, your premium jumps to at least 284.10 dollars a month, with several higher tiers after that. IRMAA is based on your tax return from two years earlier, so your 2026 premium depends on your 2024 income. If you've had a major income drop since then, like retirement, you can file an appeal with Social Security. Check your income bracket before assuming the standard premium applies to you.

The standard 2026 Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 a month (deductible $283), but IRMAA surcharges push it higher for individuals earning over $109,000 or couples over $218,000, based on income from two years prior. Here's how the brackets work and how to appeal if your income has dropped.

topics.title: 2026 American Opportunity Tax Credit: Up to $2,500 Per Student (IRS)
topics.script: Paying for college this year? Make sure you're not leaving this credit on the table. The American Opportunity Tax Credit lets you claim up to 2,500 dollars per eligible student for tuition, fees, and course materials during their first four years of college. Here's the part people miss, 40 percent of that credit, up to 1,000 dollars, is refundable, meaning you can get it back even if you owe zero in taxes. For 2026, the credit phases out once your modified adjusted gross income hits 80,000 dollars if you're single, or 160,000 if you're married filing jointly, and disappears entirely at 90,000 and 180,000. You'll need Form 8863 and a 1098-T from the school to claim it. Check your income against these numbers before you file this year's return.
topics.description:

topics.title: RMD Age Is 73 in 2026 - Miss It and Pay a 25% IRS Penalty
topics.script: If you're approaching retirement, mark this age on your calendar. Under current IRS rules, you generally must start taking required minimum distributions, or RMDs, from your traditional IRA, SIMPLE IRA, SEP IRA, or 401k once you turn 73. This age moved up thanks to the SECURE 2.0 Act, it used to be 70 and a half, then 72. The IRS calculates your RMD based on your account balance and your life expectancy factor. Here's the part that really stings, if you miss your RMD or don't take enough, the penalty is 25 percent of the amount you should have withdrawn, though it drops to 10 percent if you fix it within two years. Roth IRAs don't have this requirement during the owner's lifetime. Mark your 73rd birthday and talk to your account provider well before year end.
topics.description:

Miss the deadline and the penalty is 25% of the amount you should have withdrawn (10% if corrected within two years). Here's what changed under SECURE 2.0 and how to avoid the penalty.

topics.title: Leftover 529 Funds? Roll Up to $35,000 Into a Roth IRA Tax-Free (IRS)
topics.script: Got leftover money in a 529 college savings plan? You're not stuck with it anymore. Under current IRS rules, you can roll over up to 35,000 dollars of unused 529 funds into a Roth IRA for the same beneficiary over their lifetime, completely tax and penalty free. There are a few requirements though. The 529 account has to have been open for at least 15 years, and any contributions made in the last 5 years, plus their earnings, don't qualify for the rollover. It also has to be a direct transfer from the 529 plan to the Roth IRA, and normal annual Roth contribution limits still apply each year. This is a great option if your kid got a scholarship or didn't use all the money for school. Check with your 529 plan provider on how to start the transfer.

topics.title: First-Time Homebuyers: Pull $10,000 From Your IRA Penalty-Free (IRS Rule)
topics.script: Struggling to save for a down payment? Your IRA might be able to help. Under IRS rules, first time homebuyers can withdraw up to 10,000 dollars from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early withdrawal penalty, even if you're under 59 and a half. This is a lifetime limit, not an annual one, and it applies per person, so a married couple could potentially pull 20,000 dollars combined. You're still considered a first time buyer if you haven't owned a home in the past two years, even if you've owned one before that. Keep in mind, this exception only waives the penalty, you'll usually still owe regular income tax on a traditional IRA withdrawal, though qualified Roth IRA withdrawals may come out tax free too. This rule only applies to IRAs, not 401k plans. Talk to a financial advisor before tapping retirement funds for a home.

topics.title: Self-Employment Tax Explained: 15.3% You Might Not Be Budgeting For (IRS)
topics.script: If you freelance, drive for a gig app, or run your own business, this tax catches a lot of people off guard. The IRS self-employment tax rate is 15.3 percent, made up of 12.4 percent for Social Security and 2.9 percent for Medicare. As a W-2 employee, your employer normally pays half of these taxes for you, but when you're self-employed, you're responsible for both halves yourself. The good news, the IRS lets you deduct half of your self-employment tax when calculating your adjusted gross income, which softens the blow a little. This tax is separate from your regular income tax, so you owe both. Most self-employed people need to make quarterly estimated tax payments throughout the year to avoid a penalty. Use Schedule SE to calculate exactly what you owe.
topics.description:
The IRS self-employment tax rate is 15.3% (12.4% Social Security plus 2.9% Medicare), covering both the employee and employer portions that a traditional job would split. Here's why freelancers and 1099 workers owe this on top of regular income tax, and the deduction that softens it.

General education only, not personalized tax or financial advice. Source: IRS.gov (Topic no. 554, Self-Employment Tax). Consult a CPA for your specific situation.

topics.script: Got kids? Here's a 2026 number that matters at tax time. The IRS confirms the Child Tax Credit is now 2,200 dollars per qualifying child under 17, adjusted upward under the new tax law. This credit reduces what you owe dollar for dollar, it's not just a deduction like the standard deduction. To claim it, your child needs a valid Social Security number, needs to live with you more than half the year, and you need to fall under the income limits for your filing status. A portion of this credit can still be refundable, meaning some families get money back even if they owe zero in taxes. Pull together each child's Social Security number before you file, since the IRS requires it to claim this credit for 2026.
topics.description:
The 2026 Child Tax Credit is $2,200 per qualifying child under 17, adjusted under the new tax law. Here's how the credit works, why it's different from a deduction, and what you need before filing to claim it this year.

topics.title: 2026 Kiddie Tax Rule: First $1,350 of a Kid's Unearned Income Is Tax-Free
topics.script: If your kid has a custodial brokerage account, this 2026 rule matters. The IRS kiddie tax applies to a child's unearned income, interest, dividends, and capital gains, not wages from a job. For 2026, the first 1,350 dollars of that income is tax free. The next 1,350, so up to 2,700 total, gets taxed at the child's own lower rate. Anything above 2,700 dollars gets taxed at the parent's higher marginal rate instead. That's the whole point, stopping parents from parking investments in a kid's name to dodge taxes. This mostly hits families with custodial UTMA or UGMA accounts. Keep every 1099 your child receives each year so you don't get caught off guard at filing time.
topics.description:
For 2026, the IRS kiddie tax lets a child's first $1,350 of unearned income (interest, dividends, capital gains) go tax-free, with the next $1,350 taxed at the child's rate and anything above $2,700 taxed at the parent's rate. Here's why this rule exists and who it affects.

topics.title: 2026 QBI Deduction Phase-In: $201,750 Single / $403,500 Married (IRS)
topics.script: Run a small business, freelance, or have rental income? This 2026 number affects your tax bill. The IRS raised the income thresholds for the Qualified Business Income deduction, also called Section 199A. For 2026, the full 20 percent deduction phases in once your taxable income crosses 201,750 dollars if you're single, or 403,500 dollars if you're married filing jointly. Below those numbers, most pass-through business owners, think sole proprietors, S corporations, and partnerships, can generally deduct 20 percent of their qualified business income without extra limits. Above those thresholds, extra rules kick in based on wages paid and the type of business you run. This deduction was made permanent under the new tax law. Talk to a CPA to see how much of your business income qualifies.
topics.description:
The 2026 Qualified Business Income (Section 199A) deduction thresholds are $201,750 for single filers and $403,500 for married filing jointly, above which extra wage and business-type limits apply. Here's how this permanent 20% pass-through deduction works for small business owners.

topics.title: 2026 Net Investment Income Tax: 3.8% Above $200K/$250K (IRS)
topics.script: If you have investment income and you're a higher earner, this tax might be sneaking up on you. It's called the Net Investment Income Tax, or NIIT, and the IRS applies it at 3.8 percent on top of your regular capital gains or investment taxes. It kicks in once your modified adjusted gross income crosses 200,000 dollars if you're single or head of household, or 250,000 dollars if you're married filing jointly. It applies to the smaller of your net investment income or the amount you're over that threshold, and it covers things like interest, dividends, capital gains, and rental income. This tax has stayed at the same thresholds for years, it's not adjusted for inflation. If you're near these numbers and selling investments, this is worth running the math on first.
topics.description:
The 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) applies once modified AGI crosses $200,000 (single/head of household) or $250,000 (married filing jointly) in 2026, on interest, dividends, capital gains, and rental income. Here's how the tax is calculated and why these thresholds never move.

topics.title: 2026 Additional Medicare Tax: 0.9% Extra Above $200K (IRS Rule)
topics.script: Here's a payroll tax a lot of higher earners don't realize exists separately. It's called the Additional Medicare Tax, and the IRS charges an extra 0.9 percent on top of the regular 1.45 percent Medicare tax. It applies once your wages or self-employment income cross 200,000 dollars if you're single, 250,000 dollars if you're married filing jointly, or 125,000 if you're married filing separately. Your employer is required to start withholding this extra amount automatically once your wages with them cross 200,000 dollars, regardless of your filing status, so you might owe more or less when you file depending on your actual household numbers. If you have two jobs or you're self-employed too, double check the math yourself using Form 8959 so you're not surprised at tax time.

topics.title: EV Tax Credit Is Gone for 2026 - IRS Confirms End Date
topics.script: Thinking about buying an electric vehicle in 2026? Here's a tax break that's no longer there to help. The IRS confirms the federal Clean Vehicle Tax Credit, for new EVs, used EVs, and commercial clean vehicles, ended for any vehicle acquired after September 30th, 2025. It was eliminated under the new tax law passed in 2025, officially called the One Big Beautiful Bill. If you signed a binding purchase contract and made a payment on or before September 30th, 2025, you may still qualify even if you take delivery later, so dig up your paperwork if you were in that window. For any EV purchase from here on in 2026, don't count on a federal credit anymore. Some states, utility companies, and even manufacturers still offer their own separate EV incentives, so it's worth checking those before you buy.

The federal Clean Vehicle Tax Credit (new, used, and commercial EVs) ended for any vehicle acquired after September 30, 2025, eliminated under 2025's tax law. Here's the binding-contract exception that might still apply to you, and where to look for remaining incentives.

topics.title: 2026 SSDI Work Limit: Earn Up to $1,690/Month (SSA Number)
topics.script: If you're on Social Security Disability and thinking about working, this 2026 number is the one to know. The Social Security Administration sets a monthly earnings limit called substantial gainful activity, or SGA. For 2026, that limit is 1,690 dollars a month for most people, and 2,830 dollars a month if you're blind. Earn under that amount doing work, and it generally doesn't count against your disability eligibility. Go over it consistently, and the SSA may decide you're no longer disabled under their rules. There's also a trial work period that lets you test working for 1,210 dollars a month or more without immediately losing benefits. These numbers update most years, so if you're receiving SSDI and picking up work, check your pay against the current limit before you commit to more hours.
topics.description:
The 2026 Social Security substantial gainful activity (SGA) limit is $1,690/month for most SSDI recipients, and $2,830/month if you're blind, with a $1,210/month trial work period threshold. Here's how working while on disability affects your benefits.

topics.title: 2026 Medicare Part A: $565/Month Premium, $1,736 Deductible (CMS)
topics.script: Most people think Medicare Part A is free, and for many it is, but not everyone. Here's the 2026 numbers from CMS. If you or your spouse paid Medicare taxes for at least 10 years, 40 quarters, your Part A premium is zero. If you have between 30 and 39 quarters, you pay a reduced premium of 311 dollars a month. Under 30 quarters, the full premium is 565 dollars a month. Separately, if you're admitted to the hospital, the Part A deductible is now 1,736 dollars per benefit period, and that can apply more than once a year if you're readmitted after a 60 day gap. This deductible covers your first 60 days of inpatient care. Check your work history with Social Security if you're unsure which premium tier applies to you before you enroll.
topics.description:
For 2026, CMS set the Medicare Part A hospital inpatient deductible at $1,736 per benefit period, with premiums of $0 (40+ work quarters), $311 (30-39 quarters), or $565/month (under 30 quarters) for those who owe one. Here's how the quarters-worked rule determines what you pay.

topics.title: Child & Dependent Care Credit: $3,000 / $6,000 Expense Limit (IRS)
topics.script: Paying for daycare, a babysitter, or after school care so you can work? There's a tax credit for that, separate from a dependent care FSA at work. It's called the Child and Dependent Care Credit, and the IRS lets you count up to 3,000 dollars of care expenses for one qualifying child or dependent, or up to 6,000 dollars if you have two or more. You then get a percentage of those expenses back as a credit, based on your income, the lower your income, the higher your percentage. This covers daycare, summer day camp, and care for a dependent who can't care for themselves while you work or look for work. You'll need the care provider's tax ID to claim it on Form 2441. Check your receipts and provider info before you file this year's return.
topics.description:
The Child and Dependent Care Credit lets you count up to $3,000 in care expenses for one qualifying dependent, or $6,000 for two or more, with the credit percentage based on your income. Here's what counts as a qualifying expense and what you'll need to claim it on Form 2441.

topics.title: Unemployment Benefits Are Taxable - IRS Reporting Rule You Can't Skip
topics.script: If you collected unemployment benefits this year, don't skip this at tax time. The IRS is clear, unemployment compensation counts as taxable income, and you have to report all of it. Your state will send you a Form 1099-G showing the total amount paid to you in box one, and if you had any federal tax withheld, that shows up in box four. You report that income on Schedule 1 of your Form 1040. A lot of people don't realize taxes aren't automatically taken out of unemployment checks unless you specifically request withholding when you file your claim. That means you could owe money at tax time if you didn't plan for it. If you're currently on unemployment, log into your state's unemployment portal and opt into withholding now so you're not surprised later.
topics.description:
The IRS requires you to report all unemployment compensation as taxable income, shown in Box 1 of your Form 1099-G and reported on Schedule 1 of Form 1040. Here's why taxes often aren't withheld automatically, and how to opt into withholding before it costs you at filing time.

topics.title: Selling Your Home? Exclude Up to $250K/$500K in Gains Tax-Free (IRS)
topics.script: Selling your home this year? This IRS rule could save you a huge tax bill. If you sell your primary residence, you can exclude up to 250,000 dollars of capital gains from tax if you're single, or up to 500,000 dollars if you're married filing jointly. To qualify, you generally need to have owned the home and lived in it as your main residence for at least 2 of the last 5 years before the sale, and those two years don't have to be consecutive. You also can't have used this exclusion on a different home sale within the past two years. If your gain is bigger than these limits, only the amount above the exclusion gets taxed as a capital gain. Keep records of home improvements, they can increase your cost basis and lower your taxable gain even further.
topics.description:
The IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of home-sale capital gains ($500,000 married filing jointly) if you owned and lived in the home as your main residence for at least 2 of the last 5 years. Here's how the ownership and use tests work and why keeping improvement records matters.

General education only, not personalized tax or financial advice. Source: IRS.gov (Topic no. 701, Sale of Your Home). Consult a CPA for your specific situation.

topics.title: Lifetime Learning Credit: Up to $2,000 - Not Just for Undergrads (IRS)
topics.script: Taking classes to boost your career, even grad school or just one course? There's a tax credit for that too, and it's different from the one aimed at undergrads. The Lifetime Learning Credit lets you claim 20 percent of up to 10,000 dollars in qualified education expenses, for a maximum credit of 2,000 dollars per tax return, not per student. Unlike the American Opportunity Credit, there's no limit on how many years you can claim it, and you don't need to be pursuing a degree or going at least half time. To qualify, your modified adjusted gross income has to be under 90,000 dollars if you're single, or 180,000 dollars if you're married filing jointly. This one's great for career changers, grad students, and anyone taking a single course to upskill. Grab your 1098-T from the school before you file.

Here's who it's for and how it differs from the American Opportunity Credit.
